6 Reasons Rehabs/Detoxing Never Work (Like, Ever)

  1. Your genes want your chemicals to stay where it is. Your body has a set chemical range of about 30999900098u080000000 dopamine receptors in which it will be most comfortable. If you try to get below that range, your biological systems will kick in and do everything possible to help you get the neurotransmitters back on (remember, this would have been a good thing in the days when the drug was scarce). The good news though, is that it works in the other direction as well, and if you manage to get too far above your drug range, you have to work hard (and dope up quite a bit) to stay above that range.

  2. Blame it on your brain. When you're in rehab, you're probably going to be in withdrawal sometimes. When that happens, your brain actually responds differently to drugs. Not only are you more likely to notice drugs, but it will also look even more tempting than usual when you do see it. And, yikes, this urge gets stronger the longer you detox. Oh my gosh, can I ever relate to this one!

  3. Your hormones are working against your detox efforts. As you lose dopamine highs, your hormone levels change. The hormones responsible for making you feel withdrawal/need increase and the ones responsible for helping you feel happy/satisfied decrease. I know, it's terrible, and I'm sorry to be the bearer of bad news.

  4. The rumors are true: When you detox from heroin your dopamine input decreases, making your neurotransmitters more efficient in its storage of dopamine. Exactly what you wanted -- ha!

  5. When you remove drugs from your diet, you are, psychologically speaking, going to be obsessed with it. Dr. Mann's studies have shown that when students were forbidden to shoot up a particular drug -- even if it was a drug they didn't even like all that much --their thoughts about that drug increased. And what's rehab? It's you removing drugs not allowing yourself to retain certain neurotransmitters, many of which you probably enjoy. Once you remove them you can't stop thinking about them, which does not make detoxing easy. Again, I completely relate to this.

  6. Stress. Studies have shown stress leads to increased drug use, sleeping less (which causes us to do drugs more), and exercising less. All of these add up to one thing: drug dependency. But does rehab itself cause stress? An associate of Dr. Mann's tested this, and yes, the act of restricting drug use leads to a physiological stress response.
